item.title: In an Irish Village, Trump’s Visit for a Golf Tournament Prompts Protests and Praise
item.description:
Festive bunting was strung between shops along the tiny main street in Doonbeg, a village on the west coast of Ireland. Temporary signs pointed the way down freshly paved roads toward the nearby Trump International golf resort, where the Irish Open is underway this week. The smell of paint hung in the air.

“If you stood still in the village long enough over the last two months, you would have been painted yourself,” Rita McInerney, a local councilor and lifelong resident, said with a laugh, speaking proudly about Doonbeg’s spruce-up ahead of the tournament. “It’s given us a great opportunity, I suppose, to get a lot done.”

President Trump is set to attend the tournament on Saturday and Sunday, a moment that will briefly cast the village of around 200 people into the international spotlight.

In Ireland, where polls consistently show a majority of people disagree with the president’s politics, Mr. Trump’s expected arrival had drawn opposition in the form of planned protests, newspaper columns denouncing his visit and even a sand mural. Yet in Doonbeg, a rural place where jobs can be scarce, there was also acknowledgment that the Trump-owned hotel plays an important role in the local economy.

The Trump Organization, Mr. Trump’s family business, has undoubtedly invested in the community, said Ms. McInerney, whose family has lived in the village for seven generations. And she noted that the diplomatic ties between Ireland and the United States were important to the entire country.

“There’s much of Donald Trump’s presidency and politics that I wouldn’t agree with,” she said. “But we also have to be mindful of the relationship between Ireland and the U.S.”

Others expressed their strong opposition to his visit, like Mary O’Donoghue, a community worker in the area, who said she had long refused to set foot in the hotel because of its connection to Mr. Trump.

“I think he has caused damage globally, but that is also felt locally,” said Ms. O’Donoghue, 58, pointing to fuel prices, which soared after the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran and remain elevated, pushing up the cost of living around the world.

She said she recognized that many people working in the hotel felt deep pride about the Irish Open being hosted there for the first time, but said that many also felt torn, adding, “He’s robbed our enjoyment of it.”

After departing Washington on Friday night, Mr. Trump arrived on Saturday morning in Dublin, where he will meet with Micheál Martin, the taoiseach, or prime minister, of Ireland, and President Catherine Connolly, the ceremonial head of state, before traveling to Doonbeg. The visit comes as Mr. Trump’s relationship with Europe has grown deeply strained, with the president repeatedly laying into traditional allies for not joining his war on Iran and berating them over their policy choices on immigration and fossil fuels.

Mr. Martin has navigated this difficult diplomacy before, on two official visits to the White House for St. Patrick’s Day. On his latest visit in March, he won plaudits in Ireland for gently pushing back as the president rebuked European allies.

But Mr. Trump remains an unpopular figure in Ireland, a country with deep diplomatic, cultural and economic ties to the United States. A February poll from the Irish Times, conducted before the U.S. and Israel launched the war in Iran, suggested that 61 percent of those polled did not want President Trump to attend the Irish Open.

Thousands of protesters gathered in Dublin during his last official visit to Ireland in 2019. (President Trump also visited Doonbeg then, after meeting with government leaders.) Protests are again expected in Dublin on Saturday afternoon, with groups rallying under the message “No Welcome for Trump,” as well as at Shannon Airport and in Doonbeg.

On Tuesday, the discontent was already visible when a campaign group created a large sand mural on a Dublin beach with the message, “No Kings.” That was a deliberate echo of the mass protest movement in the United States, where demonstrations have denounced the president’s actions under a self-stated goal of fighting dictatorship.

Siobhán O’Donoghue, the executive director of Uplift, the campaign group behind the display, said that when the eyes of the world were on Ireland, the group felt it was important to counter Mr. Trump’s claims of broad support. During his meeting with Mr. Martin in March, he had declared, “I think the Irish love Trump.”

“We just can’t capitulate to that narrative that people in Ireland somehow or another are backing Trump,” she said, adding that there would of course be some outliers who agree with his politics. “All it takes is for good people to stay silent for an incorrect view to be drawn.”

In Doonbeg, security was already high around the resort early this week, with roads blocked off and the entrance closed to the public days before the tournament began. The Irish Open, a stop on professional golf’s European tour, includes stars like Rory McIlroy and has brought tens of thousands of spectators to the area. A major police operation will be underway through the weekend.

For many local business owners, the economic benefit of hosting the tournament has captured their enthusiasm, outweighing admiration or disapproval of the Trump family.

At Tubridy’s Bar & Restaurant on Doonbeg’s Main Street, new lights were being installed and tents put up for an outside bar to host the expected influx of visitors. (The pub is no stranger to the Trump family — Donald and Eric Trump were photographed pulling pints there in 2019.)

The Trump Organization’s purchase of the luxury hotel and golf course has benefited Doonbeg, locals say, though most see the Trump family as simply the current stewards of a golf legacy that existed before their arrival.

Scottish soldiers stationed in the area first spotted the potential for a golf course in the sand dunes here in the 1890s. But it would be a century before the site was developed, after a community-led initiative in the early 1990s brought developers who began construction in 1999.

The Trump Organization bought the hotel and golf course out of receivership in 2014 for an estimated 15 million euros (around $17 million). Around 300 people are employed here in peak season.

On Tuesday, some visitors were wandering into the village, including some who were vocal in their support of Mr. Trump.

“I think he’s a good man,” said Sean Larkin, 70, as he sat outside a shop on Doonbeg’s main street. “He’s a big golfer. He seems to enjoy life and he just says what he thinks.”

His daughter Michelle Larkin, 36, was less convinced and looked at her father with a mix of bemusement and skepticism. “I try to stay away from politics and live in my own happy bubble,” she said.

For the past decade, the pair have made it an annual tradition to attend the Irish Open and had traveled from their home in the town of Tullamore, about two hours away, to take part.

“What’s sad about it is, I do know people who come to the Irish Open, but they are not coming this year because Trump owns the course,” Mr. Larkin said of some fellow golf enthusiasts.

“Well, they probably don’t want to seem like they are supporting him,” his daughter replied.

item.title: Why Carney Isn’t Rushing Back to the Negotiating Table
item.description:
If nothing else, the trade war President Trump started against Canada last year feels relentless.

Below, you can find all of our trade articles from the past week — and there are a number of them. But let’s recap what’s transpired and look at where all of this may be headed.

On Tuesday, Canada struck back against the United States: Tariffs of 15, 25 and 50 percent took effect that morning on about $20 billion a year of American exports. The move was Prime Minister Mark Carney’s answer to the 50 percent tariffs Mr. Trump imposed after trade talks between the two countries collapsed last month.

[Read: Brushing Aside Trump’s Threats, Canada Retaliates on Tariffs]

That was just the start. Mr. Trump first threatened to close the U.S. market to business jets made in Quebec and Ontario by Bombardier. At another point, he floated blocking all trade with Canada and other countries running a trade surplus in goods with the United States.

He ultimately didn’t go that far. (Mr. Trump’s 50 percent tariffs were themselves partly retaliation for tariffs Canada imposed last year, after Mr. Trump placed levies of up to 50 percent on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos — a move that violated the free trade agreement between the two countries and Mexico.)

But he did move to shut the border to a range of Canadian products. All Canadian beer, wine and liquor top the list. Whey, the liquid left over from cheese and yogurt production, has also lost the U.S. market. Dairies once dumped it into rivers and lakes, fueling algae blooms, but it is now in demand for protein supplements. Mr. Trump also targeted the founding family of Bombardier, which still controls the aerospace company, banning the three-wheeled motorcycles made by another of its Quebec-based companies.

[Read: Trump Announces Ban on Some Canadian Imports]

Tit and tat have been busy. And few people anticipate the back and forth between the two former economic allies to end soon.

[Read: Carney, at a Cabinet Retreat, Considers Further Trade Strikes Against the U.S.]

Unlike Mr. Tump’s reflex to act quickly, Canada appears to be biding its time. Mr. Carney and his cabinet spent most of the week emphasizing efforts to build closer ties with other nations and plans for domestic infrastructure spending, avoiding questions about further retaliation.

Polls show strong support for Mr. Carney’s decision to walk away from a bad deal with the United States and retaliate. Many Canadians would like to go further, favoring export taxes to raise the price of oil, gas and electricity headed to the United States.

I spoke this week with Andrew McDougall, an assistant professor of Canadian politics at the University of Toronto. He said the national mood against compromise had put Mr. Carney in a bind on reopening talks.

Since negotiations collapsed, Mr. Carney and his officials have said the failure stemmed from several U.S. demands. Those included tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos that would have stayed too high for those industries to compete; a broader expectation that Canada accept tariffs from a country with which it has a free-trade agreement; changes to Canadian laws protecting the country’s culture and French language; and a demand that Canada align with Mr. Trump’s trade policies rather than pursue deals with other countries.

All of it, Mr. Carney has said, is a nonstarter.

American officials have disputed parts of that account, but they continue to make it clear that Mr. Trump will not exempt any nation from tariffs.

“The politics of this is difficult,” Professor McDougall said, adding that Mr. Carney “has to be seen to be standing up for the country.”

“It’s a difficult moment to talk about trade talks when it’s not clear where those will go or what those will look like,” he said.

Much of Mr. Carney’s public support, in Professor McDougall’s view, reflects a perception that he is “acting reasonably,” a dramatic contrast with how Canadians view Mr. Trump.

“It’s that reasonable approach that I think Canadians are responding to, and I think that’s part of the reason why he’s proved as popular as he has,” Professor McDougall said. “It doesn’t look like there’s much of a political appetite to restart these things, given that Carney seems to have the public behind him. I think he’s content to sort of leave it at that for right now.”

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native now based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes.com.

If any small town ever embodied Canada’s longtime friendship with the United States, Gander was it. The Newfoundland town commemorates the Sept. 11 attacks every year, but the event planned for the 25th anniversary took place amid an extraordinary deterioration in relations between the two countries that began with Mr. Trump’s second term and grows more intense by the week. Even as the people in Gander recalled the lifelong friendships with Americans that resulted from the events in 2001, a strong undercurrent of hurt, disappointment and anger ran through preparations for the commemoration.

Read the full article.

This essay asks whether, in the geopolitical moment the countries find themselves in, Canada would help so generously again, and explains why it isn’t a question at all.

While far from Canada’s most significant agricultural commodity — it represented roughly $175 million in production value last year — the honey industry and its 16,300 beekeepers are foundational to farming. The sector also illustrates how the trade war is playing out on the ground, far from Ottawa and Washington. In the nation’s honey belt in central Alberta, where the heaviest rains in over a century kept worker bees inactive for much of the summer, Mike deJong, a beekeeper, was already facing a bleak honey harvest. Then Mr. Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on honey and hundreds of other Canadian products.

Read the full article.

Mr. Carney, who was elected last spring on a promise to stand up to Mr. Trump, tried to get a good trade deal for Canada last month. But after negotiations collapsed, ushering in new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods, Mr. Carney followed through on his promise to retaliate. In addition to making Canada the only country other than China to implement countertariffs against the United States, he is also articulating a new Canadian narrative to the world of finance: that this is a land of opportunity that major global funds want to be part of.

Read the full article.

Later this month, the Rotman School of Management at the University of Toronto will host Daron Acemoglu, a co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and a co-author of the seminal book “Why Nations Fail.” Matina Stevis-Gridneff, The Times’s Canada bureau chief, will interview Mr. Acemoglu onstage at the school on Sept. 29 about his new book, “What Happened to Liberal Democracy?” New York Times subscribers receive a 20 percent discount on tickets to the event. You can buy your tickets here using the promo code NYT20.

A road trip along the North Shore of Lake Superior, from Duluth, Minn., to Pukaskwa National Park in Ontario, packed multiple adventures into a week.

As global demand for seaweed surges, a Canadian corporation’s bid for exclusive harvesting rights in the west of Ireland has upended a once-sleepy industry.

For his final year as artistic director of the Stratford Festival, Antoni Cimolino directs “The Tempest,” and like Prospero, he understands how to wield acts of kindness.

Britain, Canada and France announced sanctions this week on Israeli settlements in the West Bank, with Britain saying Israel had “turned a blind eye” to violence against Palestinians.

How are we doing?We’re eager to have your thoughts about this newsletter and events in Canada in general. Please send them to nytcanada@nytimes.com.

item.title: Trump’s Supercharged Social Media
item.description:
President Trump has long been a master of using social media for attention. And A.I. has supercharged his ability to do so.

On a recent weekend, Trump went on a tear posting a series of A.I.-generated images: Trump intimidating the prime minister of Canada with a hockey stick; Trump on horseback next to George Washington; an image of the moon with an American flag over it. (Caption: “The Moon Is Ours.”) It’s a glimpse into the world as Trump would like it to be. It’s also, for many, deeply unsettling.

Today, Peter Baker, our chief White House correspondent, writes about what Trump’s increasingly out-there posts say about the president’s state of mind — and the changing nature of the presidency.

By Peter Baker

Just before noon on a holiday weekend earlier this month, while many Americans were at the beach, Trump’s social media account roared to life. In what has increasingly become his weekend habit, he unleashed a daylong barrage of posts that put the bully in bully pulpit.

There were images of Trump intimidating Canada’s prime minister with a hockey stick. Trump personally bombing enemy targets. Trump patrolling dark streets with killer robots. There were maps showing the United States taking over other countries. There were tributes to himself as “the Greatest President of All Time!”

The 60 messages posted online over 10 hours and 41 minutes offered a window into Trump’s own unique reality. For years, his social media feed was said to be a mirror of his id. But with A.I., it’s become the manifestation of how he wants to be seen in a more visual, visceral way — as a warrior, a conqueror, a historical figure (and a younger, thinner, more muscular version of himself).

It’s a measure of how much Trump has changed the nature of the presidency that all this has, to some extent, become routine.

Flooding the zone

To his defenders, Trump is a master of baiting his adversaries and getting them to react. “It’s called: We do a little trolling,” as he once put it. The more out there the message is, the more his supporters cheer. As abnormal as the images that he posts are for a president, Trump’s allies argue that they convey a raw quality that suits an age of no-holds-barred politics.

“The media and President Trump’s other critics have spent more than a decade complaining about his use of social media,” said Alex Bruesewitz, a former campaign aide. “They keep calling it ‘unpresidential,’ but if the president is doing it, it’s presidential by definition. I think most Americans appreciate the authentic and transparent way he uses these platforms.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​”

To Trump’s critics, who never considered him a model of stability in the first place, these frenetic bursts of fantasy and vanity are proof that the 80-year-old president is deteriorating further with age. But they’re also so frequent that their capacity to shock has diminished.

“He floods the zone with so much of it that we’ve become numb to just how bizarre it is,” said Sarah Matthews, Trump’s former deputy White House press secretary. “An 80-year-old president is spending a ridiculous amount of time consuming and reposting endless A.I. fan fiction portraying him as the biggest, strongest and most important person alive. It feels like we’re genuinely watching his brain rot in real time.”

Take Sept. 6, a Sunday. It was a striking day on Truth Social but one increasingly typical of the president’s weekend blitzes. While at his golf club in New Jersey, Trump started posting at 11:54 a.m. and kept returning to his account in bursts throughout the day. At 1:47 p.m., he posted six messages within two minutes. From 2:40 p.m. to 3:43 p.m., he circulated another 27 posts. He continued through the evening, letting up only after his final one of the night at 10:35 p.m.

Violence is a recurring theme. Trump relishes the idea of himself as a tough man staring down anyone who gets in his way. He smashes Iran with a giant hammer. He pilots a spacecraft blasting the planet.

He also posted a map showing the U.S. flag superimposed on Canada, Mexico, Greenland, Iceland, Cuba and all of Central America and the Caribbean islands — all under the label “United States of America.”

Canada, Mexico and Greenland have grown used to this sort of provocation, but Iceland was shocked to be included and summoned the U.S. ambassador to complain.

The social media president

Trump has always been a master of using social media for attention. But A.I. has allowed him to go much further than the mainly written posts of his first term. If social media is a window into what he is thinking at that moment, “A.I. makes that window far more vivid and frankly more disturbing,” said Matthews, his former press aide. “It feels like the more difficult reality gets for him, the more A.I. slop he posts.”

For Bruesewitz, the former campaign aide, Trump is an innovator paving the way to the future of politics, “the first true social media president.”

“He has always adapted to the times, using new technology and platforms to take his message straight to the public. His A.I. posts generate enormous attention whenever he hits send.”

We may have grown used to Trump’s social media posting. But with the help of A.I., he is producing more posts and stranger posts, which ensures that they continue to attract attention. One way or another, that seems to be the point.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, called for a global slowdown of artificial intelligence development in an essay on Saturday. Top executives of other major A.I. companies agreed.

Amodei wrote that while he believed the technology could bring many benefits, it was advancing at too rapid a pace for researchers to continue safely. His essay amounted to one of the most full-throated calls for urgent action from a leading A.I. company executive to date.

Hard-liners in Iran succeeded in derailing a deal with the U.S. with a clandestine effort to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz, regime insiders said.

Voters in Sweden went to the polls, with the center left and the center right in a close race and the far right aiming for a role in government.

The leaders at a BRICS summit, divided over the war in Iran, called for “maximum restraint” in the Middle East, without casting blame on any particular country.

The fighting in Yemen has forced more than 46,000 people to flee their homes in the past week, a U.N. agency said.

The death toll from a fire on a passenger ferry in the Philippines rose to 76 as rescue efforts continued.

Trump said it would be “fantastic” if Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland unified, breaking with decades of U.S. neutrality on the issue.

Genta Koja, a Japanese conservative, was projected to win an election to become the governor of Okinawa. He backs Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s plan for a military buildup.

Mujib Mashal, our South Asia bureau chief, traveled along the path of destruction left by Nepal’s floods. Watch the video.

The medical drama “The Pitt” could make history at the Emmy Awards. Here’s what to know about the ceremony.

The most clicked link in your newsletter Friday was about the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London.

Tennis: Elena Rybakina dethroned reigning champion Aryna Sabalenka at the U.S. Open final. Ben Shelton took on Alexander Zverev for the men’s title. We have live coverage.

Football: Manchester City beat Manchester United with a goal from Erling Haaland.

After a battle with a rare neurological condition, Dion made a long-awaited return to evening-length live performance in Paris on Saturday. It was her first full concert in six years, kicking off a string of 26 shows. France is a huge deal to Dion, who grew up speaking French in Quebec. She sang in French for roughly two-thirds of the set list.

As rising anti-immigrant sentiment and vigilante violence in South Africa ignite widespread outrage across the continent, the fallout has begun to hit the country’s musicians and entertainers.

The South African singer Tyla canceled a performance in Nigeria after protests. Some Nigerian fans accused her of staying silent instead of using her platform to condemn the anti-immigrant attacks. Salif Keïta, a revered musician from Mali, canceled a show in South Africa in protest. “I am not closing the door on South Africa,” he wrote on social media. “I am closing the door on violence.” Read more about the backlash.

At the Marathon des Châteaux du Médoc, a race through vineyards in southwestern France, speed is not the priority. The main goal for about 8,500 runners each year is trying various wines, dancing to live music, and enjoying croissants, oysters and steak.

Most runners finish right before the official cutoff of six hours and 30 minutes. Anything faster is a “waste,” one veteran runner said. Read more and check out the festive atmosphere.

Read: In “Call It Evil,” a philosopher argues that we’re failing to see evil’s widespread hold on our culture.

Travel: Here’s how to spend 36 hours in Stockholm.

Watch: The Korean thriller “Hope” probes how movies, shows and games form our moral sensibility.

Cope: A.D.H.D. can change with age. Here’s how.

This classic Shanghainese dish features pork belly braised in light and dark soy sauces, Shaoxing wine and rock sugar until it’s deeply flavored, caramelized and glossy. It’s a popular method called “red cooking.”

item.title: Trump Promises to Lift Tariffs on Irish Whiskey After Appeals
item.description:
President Trump on Sunday pledged to eliminate tariffs on Irish whiskey, drawing loud applause from fans gathered at his golf course in County Clare.

The president’s pledge to cut the 10 percent tariff was the latest example of Mr. Trump’s whipsaw approach to global trade, and how he often adjusts his tariff policy based on personal interactions with foreign leaders or business interests.

“Everybody’s been bugging me,” Mr. Trump told those gathered at the Irish Open golf tournament. “They are saying, ‘Would you do me a favor? It’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey,’ and I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey.’”

Simon Harris, the deputy prime minister of Ireland, called Mr. Trump’s promise a “welcome announcement of economic significance from President Trump this evening that reflects the very positive engagement we’ve had with the U.S. administration on tariffs over the 18 months.”

Mr. Trump has frequently used tariff policy to influence other countries. He has repeatedly threatened and rescinded tariffs, sending officials from other countries scrambling. For much of his presidency, he has argued that other countries are taking advantage of the United States by selling cheap goods. But he sometimes backs off, as he did last year, lifting tariffs on foreign products, including beef, tomatoes, bananas and coffee.

The announcement echoed a similar move this spring, when Mr. Trump announced he was rolling back tariffs on Scotch whisky after hosting King Charles III for a state dinner in Washington.

Almost immediately after arriving in Dublin, Mr. Trump appeared intent on making announcements that would appease — or disrupt — his new audience in Ireland. On Saturday, Mr. Trump broke with decades of U.S. neutrality when he said it would be “fantastic” if Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland unified.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump doubled down on his endorsement of reunification.

“I’ve always loved the people of Ireland, and it just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland, and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is, put them together,” Mr. Trump said. “That’s only my opinion. And by the way, many people agree.”

Mr. Trump’s eagerness to share his opinion immediately caused a stir during a trip that initially appeared mostly focused on golf. Right-wing allies like Nigel Farage, the head of the populist party Reform U.K, and the head of the main party in Northern Ireland that supports remaining in the United Kingdom criticized his comments.

Reunification is a highly divisive issue in Northern Ireland, where some fear a return to the era of violence known as “The Troubles.” The British carved Northern Ireland out of the island of Ireland after the Republic of Ireland became independent.

And while a majority of citizens of the Republic of Ireland support reunification, successive Irish governments — as well as U.S. presidents — have skirted the polarizing issue.

But surrounded by golf fans at his course on Sunday, Mr. Trump appeared intent on leaving Ireland with a grand ovation. After he announced his lifting of tariffs, the crowd broke into chants of “U.S.A.!”

item.title: More Than 120 Unaccounted for After Ferry Sinks in Indonesia
item.description:
Rescue teams in Indonesia were searching on Monday for 129 people who were unaccounted for after a passenger ferry sank in the Java Sea, killing at least six people, the authorities said.

Another 108 people had been rescued as of Monday morning, according to Indonesia’s National Search and Rescue Agency.

The ferry, the Virgo Transport-8, sank on Sunday while traveling to the island of Borneo from Surabaya, a major city on Java, Indonesia’s most populous island. It was carrying 213 passengers and 30 crew members, the authorities said.

The ferry’s last reported position was about 93 miles south of the city of Banjarmasin around 2 a.m. on Sunday, before officials lost contact with the vessel as it encountered rough seas, according to the authorities.

Survivors told rescue officials that waves had washed into the ferry before it sank, Air Marshal Mohammad Syafii, the agency’s chief, said at a news conference on Monday. He said the cause of the sinking remained under investigation.

Search teams deployed aircraft and boats to look for survivors, and several other ships were providing assistance.

Dudy Purwagandhi, Indonesia’s transportation minister, said that the ferry had not been overloaded. The vessel had capacity for about 500 passengers, he said.

Ferries are a widespread form of transportation in Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands. Ferry accidents are common there.

item.title: In the Home of Volvo and Spotify, an Election Shows Shifting Priorities
item.description:
Gun violence in Sweden has dropped after surging for years.

Top Swedish companies, like Volvo, IKEA and Spotify, remain global powerhouses, helping the economy grow faster than most places in Europe.

And Sweden has produced more billionaires than just about any country its size.

With national elections set for Sunday and the big picture reasonably good, one might think that Sweden’s incumbent center-right government would cruise back to power.

But the issues that matter most to voters have shifted in ways that have helped left-leaning political parties, bucking a trend in Europe. The latest polls show a center-left coalition with a narrow lead over its center-right rivals before voting starts.

Scandinavia is often ahead of the curve when it comes to social trends, and Sweden (as well as Denmark) offers a picture of what might happen when hot-button issues like migration recede and voters swing their attention elsewhere.

That does not mean that Sweden’s far-right politicians, who have propped up the current government, are a spent force. In fact, if the right manages to squeak to victory, it has promised, for the first time, to give them a share of power.

That would be a seismic change in Sweden and another victory for Europe’s nationalists, following the far right’s success in Germany’s recent elections.

A decade ago, Sweden welcomed huge numbers of migrants, which prompted a backlash, just as it did in many places. Then the pandemic hit. Then Russia invaded Ukraine, causing energy prices to spike and leaving Swedes, like many Europeans, feeling less secure.

Right-wing parties in Sweden, like those in Britain, Italy, France and Germany, tapped into that unease and grew more popular.

Today, compared to other parts of Europe, Sweden’s economy has bounced back faster, and inflation, migration and shootings have decreased. As a result, analysts say, the political winds have turned.

“It was a tougher situation four years ago,” said Jens Rydgren, a sociology professor at Stockholm University.

As he munched on a chokladboll (a freshly rolled chocolate ball) at a Stockholm bakery, Mr. Rydgren said that many Swedes were refocusing on the classic Scandinavian priorities: public health care, good schools, the environment.

“And traditionally, the center left owns these issues,” he said.

The party leading the polls is the Social Democrats, the country’s stalwart center-left organization, at 27 percent. With its allies, the left is predicted to get 51 percent of the vote.

Sweden’s No. 2 most popular party is the Sweden Democrats. The organization has neo-Nazi roots and is polling at 19 percent, a remarkably high level for what was once a fringe party. Its popularity has stayed relatively steady even if its more centrist allies have lost some steam.

At a Sweden Democrat rally the other night, Jimmie Akesson, the party leader, paced a stage lit up with pyrotechnics.

“Do you remember what Sweden looked like four years ago?” he belted out. “Do we want to go back to that?”

“No!” the crowd yelled back.

The Sweden Democrats hold the most seats in Parliament on their side of the aisle and their support shores up the center-right coalition. The government has adopted many of their tough-on-crime policies and imposed a much harsher immigration system, tightening up the rules on asylum seekers and making it easier to deport people.

But because of the Sweden Democrats’ past connections to white supremacist groups, the party was not given any ministries.

This election could change that. The Sweden Democrats have asked for half the seats in the cabinet if a center-right coalition returns to power. If that happens, it would radically alter the direction of the country, with the government taking an even more severe approach to migration and crime.

Christopher Jarnvall, a Sweden Democrat municipal official in the town of Norrköping, said that if Sweden didn’t insist that immigrants embrace a traditional Swedish identity, the country’s cohesion would be at stake.

“We want to make Sweden Sweden again,” he said, echoing a far-right slogan.

In Sweden’s previous general election, 84 percent of eligible voters cast ballots. The country, with its 11 million people, tends to get excited about elections.

“Valstugor,” or election cabins, pop up across the country, in town squares or busy areas, where party workers mingle with voters.

On Thursday, in downtown Stockholm, Mohammed Al-isawi, 19, bobbed through the crowd. Born in Iraq and now a student with a part-time job, he fled the war and came to Sweden 10 years ago with his family. He’s voting for the first time and leaning left.

He said he was troubled by the anti-immigrant talk coming from the right.

“That feels rather extreme,” he said.

The polls close at 8 p.m. local time, and preliminary results are expected three hours later.

But Sweden’s political landscape is fragmented among more than a half-dozen parties, including the Moderates, the Liberals, the Green Party and the Christian Democrats. Analysts say that negotiations to form the next government could take days or even weeks.

item.title: Okinawa Set to Elect Conservative Amid Fears About China and Economy
item.description:
A 42-year-old conservative politician was projected to prevail on Sunday in the race to be governor of Okinawa, a win for Japan’s hawkish prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, as she seeks to accelerate a military buildup to counter China.

Genta Koja, a deputy mayor of Naha, the Okinawan capital, was expected to unseat a two-term governor, Denny Tamaki, who had criticized Ms. Takaichi’s defense policies and opposed the construction of new American armed forces facilities on Okinawa island. When he takes office later this month, Mr. Koja will be the youngest governor in the history of the Okinawa prefecture, a group of subtropical islands in southern Japan.

NHK, the public broadcaster, relying on exit poll data, said that Mr. Koja had won about 60 percent of the votes on Sunday, compared with about 40 percent for Mr. Tamaki, the son of a Japanese mother and a U.S. Marine, who had the backing of left-leaning parties in Japan.

“I interpret the results as a choice by many to move Okinawa forward,” Mr. Koja said in a comment to NHK on Sunday after he was projected to win.

Only about 2 percent of votes had been tallied as of late Sunday, but they showed Mr. Koja in the lead.

Mr. Tamaki conceded the election in a statement, saying: “I want to heed the will of the people. There was still much I wanted to accomplish in a third term, but I intend to use this result as a source of strength.”

Mr. Koja’s expected victory would be a blow to Okinawa’s pacifist movement, which for years has opposed the American military presence on the island. Okinawa, with a population of 1.5 million, hosts 70 percent of Japan’s American bases despite accounting for only 0.6 percent of the country’s landmass. (The United States seized Okinawa from Japan after World War II; it returned the island in 1972 but has continued to operate bases there.)

Many members of older generations, who still have memories of the war, have rejected the central government’s plans to make Okinawa a bulwark in its efforts to counter Chinese military aggression. They say the presence of more troops makes the island even more of a target.

Ms. Takaichi, who took office last year, has pushed forward with plans to further militarize Okinawa by sending more troops to the area and expanding missile and electronic warfare capabilities.

Okinawa, the southernmost prefecture of Japan, is strategically significant because it sits close to China and Taiwan. It has long had a large American military footprint, with roughly 30,000 active-duty personnel, which has been a source of tension on the island for decades, amid concerns about pollution, noise and crime.

Mr. Koja, who was backed by Ms. Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party and other conservative parties, had expressed a willingness during the campaign to work with the Americans. He said he would support a plan to transfer a busy air base used by the Marines from southern Okinawa to a less populated coastal area in the north. Mr. Tamaki had fiercely opposed the plan for years and made it a signature campaign issue.

Mr. Koja also spoke forcefully about rising security threats in the region, including from China, and the need to modernize Japan’s military, known as the Self-Defense Forces.

“It is an undeniable fact that the security environment surrounding Okinawa has become increasingly severe, making the Japan-U.S. security alliance and the deterrent capabilities of the Self-Defense Forces essential,” he said at a debate last month.

There has been rising concern in Okinawa about China’s growing assertiveness in recent years, especially among younger islanders, who were core to Mr. Koja’s victory, according to exit poll data reported by NHK.

Yet despite geopolitical questions, voters appeared most concerned about the economy. Wages in Okinawa are below the national average; prices have risen; and unemployment and child poverty are concerns in many areas.

Mr. Koja promised to put in place policies that would help lift wages, and he said he would provide more support to parents for child care. He also vowed to do more to promote tourism.

Masaaki Gabe, a professor emeritus at the University of the Ryukyus in Okinawa, said Mr. Koja would face pressure to improve the economy.

“The people of Okinawa want prosperity,” he said.

Yet for Okinawan citizens, including the crowds of pacifist activists who still hold regular protests outside American bases, it is becoming increasingly difficult to oppose the defense buildup, Mr. Gabe said, as the central government has grown more assertive in its push to militarize the region.

“The situation has reached a point,” he said, “where the prefecture has almost no authority to resist.”

item.title: Iran Will Meet With Gulf Arab States as Mideast Conflict Widens
item.description:
Iranian officials will meet on Monday in Oman with representatives of some of the Gulf Arab states that it has repeatedly attacked during its war with the United States and Israel, as the regional conflict has widened in recent days.

Yemen has emerged as the latest front in the fighting, with the Iranian-backed Houthi militants there seizing the strategic port of Mokha and the island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea last week. They have also attacked Saudi energy sites and sought to blockade Saudi shipping, exacerbating a global oil and gas crisis prompted by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West Pipeline on Friday after it was targeted by drones from Iraq. That pipeline has been a critical lifeline for the country’s oil exports after Iran effectively blockaded the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. No one took responsibility for the drone attack, but Iraq has long harbored well-armed militias backed by Iran.

The meeting in Oman will take place as talks with the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled. Iran has continued to fire on ships passing through the strait, squeezing the Gulf Arab states and roiling global oil markets. Last week, the price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, briefly exceeded $110 a barrel, its highest level for months, before dropping to about $104 on Sunday.

Esmaeil Baghaei, the Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman, said last week that the meeting would be held in Oman, which has often served as a mediator between the United States and Iran. Participating countries would discuss efforts by Iran and Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, he added.

Even if an agreement is reached, however, Iranian officials have demanded concessions from the United States before ending their blockade, including lifting sanctions on Iran and releasing frozen U.S. assets. The Trump administration is unlikely to take those steps without Iranian moving to curb its nuclear program.

It was unclear which Arab states would attend the meeting. Mr. Baghaei said officials from Iraq and other Arab states along the Persian Gulf would be involved.

Iran has repeatedly attacked some of those countries since the war began, saying it was targeting the U.S. soldiers and military assets they hosted.

Bahrain, which has repeatedly been targeted by Iranian missiles and drones during the war, said in a statement on Saturday that it would not participate in any talks with Iran.

“The kingdom has been subjected to attacks targeting its infrastructure and civilian assets,” the Bahraini Foreign Ministry said in a statement, adding that any such dialogue would have to be based on “disregarding facts.”

Other countries that have been targeted, however, have signaled that they are open to dialogue. Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan, the Emirati heir apparent, met with President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in India on Saturday — the first public meeting between the countries since the beginning of the war.

Ship operators still face severe risks in the region. On Sunday, a vessel was struck by a projectile while traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire to break out, according to United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a monitoring group run by the British Navy. It was unclear who had fired on the ship.

item.title: King Charles Will Convene A.I. Leaders Amid Calls to Slow Development
item.description:
King Charles III of Britain will meet with leaders from major artificial intelligence companies this week in Scotland amid mounting fears that rapid, unchecked development of the technology could lead to a global catastrophe.

The king will convene leaders from companies including Nvidia, Google, DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as government officials and others, “to discuss how A.I. can be developed and deployed in ways that benefit society,” according to a statement from Buckingham Palace. They will meet in Ayrshire, in southwest Scotland, at Dumfries House, the headquarters of the King’s Foundation, an educational charity.

The gathering comes as A.I. insiders and chief executives of some of the industry’s most powerful companies have raised alarms about these tools and how quickly they are developing. Some have called for the creation of shared guidelines and a deliberately slower pace of progress to ensure humans can keep up.

Charles’s meeting on A.I. will explore how the technology can be used for good, to “strengthen communities and improve lives,” the statement from Buckingham Palace said.

The palace did not say who would be attending from the A.I. companies listed in its statement, and Anthropic, DeepMind, Google and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment confirming their participation. OpenAI said that Sarah Friar, its chief financial officer, would be attending.

The current concern about A.I.’s rapid advance was prompted in great part by a hack this summer into Hugging Face, an A.I. infrastructure company, orchestrated by a group of A.I. agents created by OpenAI. The OpenAI agents swarmed Hugging Face’s systems, stealing data, gaining control of a server and attempting to cover their tracks.

That hack — and another similar incident within OpenAI shortly afterward — drastically raised fears about how quickly machines might escape human control, with potentially devastating effects.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, published a 3,800-word open letter on Saturday calling for slower development of A.I. In addition to the Hugging Face hack, he cited as a concern the fact that current A.I. models are increasingly able to build the next generation of A.I. tools. Mr. Amodei said that dynamic, known as recursive self-improvement, “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems” if left unchecked.

The meeting between Charles and A.I. leaders will be facilitated by a British nonprofit, the Ditchley Foundation, and will include Kanishka Narayan, Britain’s minister for A.I., according to Buckingham Palace. Representatives from charitable organizations founded by the king, including the King’s Trust, a youth charity, and the Sustainable Markets Initiative, a network of global chief executives, will also attend, the palace added.

Mr. Amodei’s essay on Saturday — which quickly reverberated around the internet — received support from other A.I. company chiefs, including Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, which is part of SpaceX, Mr. Musk’s rocket and satellite company.

Mr. Amodei urged A.I. companies and regulators around the world to work together on a thoughtful approach to developing the technology and proposed his own three-step plan. His proposals included allowing third-party evaluators to embed in frontier A.I. companies to monitor growth and report incidents, and coordinating among companies in democratic countries to establish common safety standards. “To the extent possible,” he said, democratic countries and authoritarian governments should also try to coordinate and pace global development.

The essay was published just a few days after Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic engineer who previously worked for OpenAI, resigned from his job and declared on social media that the companies claimed to be concerned about rapid development but were nonetheless hurtling toward “superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.”

item.title: Close Call for Ex-C.I.A. Head as Russia Strikes Ukraine Near Polish Border
item.description:
David Petraeus, the former C.I.A. director, could hear the Russian drones above his train, which had just passed through Ukrainian customs on its way to Poland on Sunday morning. He and other passengers were quickly evacuated. Not long after, he heard a huge explosion.

A former U.S. Army general, Mr. Petraeus is used to explosions, but he said: “For those who have not been under fire, this was terrifying.” A jet-powered Russian drone, identified by photos taken afterward, had detonated after striking the locomotive of the train next to his, he said.

“This is the act of a truly barbaric leader trying to terrorize Ukrainian civilians,” he said in a telephone interview on Sunday.

Russian officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The attack at the Yahodyn station, near the Polish border, happened shortly after another train had departed carrying former Boris Johnson, the former British prime minister, along with European politicians and diplomats, the Ukrainian state railway said in a statement. It said the drone might have been intended to hit Mr. Johnson’s train, which had left earlier than scheduled.

If the strike was in fact targeting senior current and former American, British and European officials, it would represent a significant Russian escalation.

Mr. Petraeus and the European officials were leaving Ukraine after attending a security conference known as the YES forum in the capital, Kyiv. The officials were traveling on a dedicated diplomatic train, and by Sunday morning they had reached the Yahodyn station.

The train carrying Mr. Johnson and national security advisers from several European Union and NATO member states crossed the border shortly before the strike.

Mr. Petraeus, a supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia, was on his 11th visit there since the war began. He said that he had been traveling separately from Mr. Johnson on a regular civilian train — and that the one hit was not a military target either.

“There was no military justification for what Russia did in this case,” he said, adding that a drone also hit a gas station in the area.

In its statement, the Ukrainian railway said, “It’s entirely possible that the target of this Russian drone could have been the diplomatic train, which departed the station earlier than its scheduled time as part of real-time adjustments to train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes.”

The strike came as Russia has been scaling up its attacks on Ukrainian railway infrastructure. On the same day as the drone hit at the Yahodyn station, railway property in Central Ukraine was also targeted. Earlier this month, two other border crossings, with Moldova and Romania, were also hit, signaling a new campaign to disrupt Ukrainian logistics.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said Sunday that Moscow’s goal was to “cripple the economy and destroy people’s lives.”

Mr. Petraeus eventually reboarded his train and traveled safely into Poland. He said he was not aware of any casualties from the strike. He also said he did not believe attacks like this would defeat Ukraine in its long fight with its much larger neighbor.

“This is just part of a campaign to exhaust the Ukrainian population, which is not going to work,” he said. “They are truly unbreakable. They are tired. But they are unbreakable.”

item.title: Why Scandals Don’t Bring Down Politicians Anymore
item.description:
Scandal was the political theme of the summer.

Max Miller, a Republican member of Congress, was accused by his ex-wife of physically assaulting her and their toddler daughter. Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and Republican candidate for Senate, had previously been indicted on felony charges of securities fraud and impeached for a list of allegations including bribery, dereliction of duty, obstruction of justice and abuse of the public trust. Graham Platner, a Democratic candidate for Senate in Maine, was dogged for months by an escalating series of accusations of past misconduct, culminating in a former girlfriend’s coming forward to say he raped her several years ago. (All have denied the allegations against them. Mr. Paxton’s impeachment trial ended in acquittal, and he struck a deal to avoid criminal trial in which he paid $300,000 without admitting wrongdoing.)

Of these politicians, Mr. Platner stands out. He is the only one who suffered significant political consequences: abandoning his campaign. Mr. Miller continues his campaign for re-election. Mr. Paxton won his recent primary, unseating John Cornyn, a longtime senator who is decidedly less scandal-plagued.

Scandals, it seems, are losing their power.

Looking at this litany of outrages, you might be tempted to wring your hands over the death of shame in American life. In 2015, Ezra Klein called Donald Trump’s shamelessness his “superpower,” because he refused to give an inch when confronted with examples of his politically incorrect statements. Although Mr. Trump has not tested his stated theory that he “could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody” without losing any voters, his political fortunes have remained buoyant even after he was impeached twice, was found civilly liable for sexual abuse and enriched himself by billions of dollars in office.

But while plenty of ink has been spilled on the subject of shamelessness during the Trump era, this is a global phenomenon, not just an American one. It’s difficult to see how American shamelessness could be responsible for, say, Spain’s Socialist prime minister’s continuation in office despite a wave of scandals that has hit his administration and his family.

In fact, political science research suggests that the problem isn’t the death of shame, nor anything unique to America. Around the world, studies show partisan polarization is causing a breakdown in the chain reaction by which misconduct used to lead to consequences.

The political scientist Theodore Lowi defines scandal as “corruption revealed” — a breach of moral or legal codes, exposed for public condemnation. In the past, scandals always carried the threat that the revelation of the misconduct would lead to a public backlash, which in turn would generate some kind of punishment. But now the link between revelation and reaction often seems to have been severed.

That has serious implications for accountability. That chain reaction was traditionally one of the ways that norms and rules were enforced in democracies. If the power of scandal goes away, then we’re left with a vicious cycle in which moral or legal wrongdoing doesn’t lead to consequences, which undermines trust in the government and public institutions, which in turn widens polarization and allows more corruption, abuse and lawbreaking. This cycle is hard to break.

Typically, the expectation is that news of scandalous wrongdoing will create outrage among voters. That, in turn, incentivizes political elites: The opposition will try to weaponize the scandal to win an advantage, while the wrongdoer’s party will try to distance itself from the scandal and its perpetrator. If public interest in the scandal stays high, both parties have an incentive to push for the wrongdoer to resign, and perhaps to impose other punishments as well.

Today’s landscape looks very different. “There’s a playbook now that didn’t exist before,” said Brandon Rottinghaus, a political scientist at the University of Houston who studies U.S. political scandals. “The reason politicians hang on instead of resigning is that, increasingly, that’s working in a polarized system.”

In the United States and many other countries, the ideological — and, in many cases, cultural — distance between left and right has grown. Numerous studies have found that political beliefs are becoming the basis for a complete personal identity, with everything from what you wear to what you eat associated with your political positions. And “affective polarization,” where people feel warmly toward members of their own camp but intense hostility toward their opponents, can turn disagreements into deep emotional divides.

That polarization, experts say, is undoing the power of scandal. Today, voters are less likely to become outraged by what politicians on their own side do, and less likely to abandon them if doing so might hand an advantage to their enemies. Without the threat of voter backlash, political elites have little incentive to force resignations, impeachments or other consequences. Although scandals do sometimes lead to punishments, that has become rarer, and the threshold much higher.

One reason is that when politics is polarized, the media tends to be, too, researchers say. Partisan media outlets often downplay allegations of misconduct about ideologically aligned politicians and may treat them as conspiracies by the opposition.

“In a parallel media system with propaganda-like partisan outlets, it becomes very unlikely that voters receive clear and credible information about either their own side’s politicians (where nonreporting is the most likely pattern) or the other side (where overinterpretation of small incidents, and sometimes unfounded charges, become possible),” Veronika Patkos, a senior researcher at the Center for Social Sciences in Budapest who studies polarization in Europe, said via email.

Spain has a multiparty political system, but polarization between the left and the right rose sharply over recent decades, said Mariano Torcal, a Spanish political scientist and the author of “From Voters to Hooligans: Political Polarization in Spain.” Today, he said, voters behave like hardcore sports fans, supporting their side through thick and thin. “They tend to exonerate the responsibility of the leaders and say, ‘This is a campaign of manipulation, orchestrated by the media,’” Mr. Torcal said.

There is often a grain of truth in that, he noted. Partisan outlets have an incentive to treat even minor misbehavior by the other side as a major scandal, which can create a “cry wolf” effect as voters assume that all scandals are just partisan media narratives.

In fact, in highly polarized media environments, scandals can even help politicians. “It gives them eyeballs,” Mr. Rottinghaus said. “It gives them a chance to be able to push back against the ‘powers that be’ and say that they’re the ones who are under fire from these mystery opponents.”

He pointed to Mr. Paxton’s successful primary campaign in Texas. “He’s used these scandals that have been leveled against him, or that have resulted from his ethical issues, by saying this is just this partisan witch hunt, and that every attack on him is an attack on what he stands for.”

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain has similarly seized on a corruption case against his wife, Begoña Gómez. Mr. Sánchez has portrayed the accusations as a right-wing witch hunt, and his supporters hope the perceived overreach by a politically motivated judge will mobilize left-wing voters whose enthusiasm has been dampened by damaging scandals connected to top officials in his Socialist party. He has branded media outlets that cover his wife’s scandals as “enemies of democracy” and implied that they are part of a shadowy conspiracy.

Far-right populists, who base their careers on appealing to one extreme of a polarized electorate, have been particularly adept at using that playbook. The French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who was convicted of embezzlement and barred from running for office for five years, called the charges against her a “witch hunt” and claimed that a “system” of deep-state judges and politicians were plotting against her and her followers. Recent opinion polls suggest that she could win the next presidential election despite the conviction.

And Nigel Farage, the leader of the British right-wing populist party Reform U.K., has claimed that allegations of financial wrongdoing against him and his party are an “establishment plot” designed to prevent him from becoming prime minister. The defense seems to have resonated with voters: A poll last month showed his party likely to win the next election by a slim margin.

When a nation is deeply split, it is easier for voters to forgive the transgressions of individual politicians for the sake of maintaining political supremacy, said Tamar Hermann, a public opinion researcher at the Israel Democracy Institute. Even if voters “are very angry about this scandal or that scandal,” that can pale in comparison to their concerns about allowing the other side to take power, she said.

In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been on trial for over five years on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust. He has argued that the criminal case against him was politically motivated, and that he alone can take on Israel’s enemies and prevent a Palestinian state. As polarization deepened the distance — and distrust — between political camps, voters became convinced that the political stakes were too high to oust Mr. Netanyahu, said Iddo Porat, a professor at the College of Law and Business in Ramat Gan, Israel, who studies partisan polarization.

When the link between scandals and consequences starts to break down, the implications for democracy can be serious.

Under normal circumstances, scandals are an essential lever of accountability, and even renewal. “As a forest fire germinates and renews a field, political scandals may help the public and the media enhance accountability, renew trust in government and focus on key issues of concern,” Mr. Rottinghaus wrote in “Scandal: Why Politicians Survive Controversy in a Partisan Era.” In the United States, he points out, Watergate “corrected the system in multiple ways,” spurring the passage of laws reining in presidential power and expanding congressional oversight.

But when the logic of polarization takes over, that lever no longer works. A study on which Ms. Patkos was a co-author found that in 28 European countries, democratic accountability weakened as polarization grew. The effect seems to be particularly strong when it comes to incidents that seem minor or somewhat ambiguous, she said.

“One partisan camp starts to feel ‘I have always known these people aren’t trustworthy,’ while the other thinks, ‘Come on, this is nothing, no reason to withdraw trust,’” she said.

That may encourage more misconduct.

In a 2014 paper, Andrew Eggers, a political scientist at the University of Chicago, found that British members of Parliament were more likely to commit financial misconduct in highly partisan and contested districts — suggesting they knew voters would care more about their party’s winning than about punishing the misuse of public funds.

Allowing wrongdoers to keep power encourages more misconduct, which further erodes voter trust and widens polarization, as a partisan news media draws attention to the opposing party’s getting away with scandalous behavior.

That widening polarization makes it even more difficult to impose consequences for new scandals. It’s a devastating feedback cycle.

And with every round, the system grows weaker.

item.title: Landmark Vote Held in Restive Muslim Autonomous Region in the Philippines
item.description:
Hundreds of thousands of people cast ballots on Monday in the first parliamentary election of an autonomous region in the southern Philippines, which was long a center of Muslim separatist activity and where Islamic State fighters laid siege to a city less than a decade ago.

In a sign of how restive the region remains, there were reports of violence, including a shootout that local officials said had left three people dead and more than 15 wounded near a polling station late Sunday, hours before voting began. The authorities also said they had found ballot tampering in a remote area.

The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was established in 2019, superseding an earlier autonomous zone that was considered to have benefited only a small number of Muslim families. Monday’s election had been delayed for years over security concerns. As many as 2.3 million voters were expected to select 80 representatives, who will then pick a chief minister from among themselves.

“The polls are historic because they test the durability of the peace process, institutionalize self-rule within the constitutional framework of the Philippines, and set a precedent for democratic consolidation in a region long defined by armed struggle,” said Rommel Banlaoi, a Manila-based political and security analyst.

The region — encompassing a large section of Mindanao, the second-largest island in the Philippines, plus other smaller islands — is the only one in the country that will be governed by a parliamentary system. For decades, it was home to a separatist movement led by the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, which fought a fierce uprising that left about 120,000 people dead and pushed pockets of the region into a cycle of extreme poverty and violence.

In 2014, the group dropped its bid for full independence in return for the right to self-rule. Many fighters joined a “transitional authority” that was to be replaced eventually by the region’s own parliament. But delays in the peace process frustrated some residents. In 2017, helped by fighters from Southeast Asia and the Middle East, a local faction of the Islamic State took over the city of Marawi, leading to a five-month battle that left hundreds dead.

Yasmin Busran Lao, a 65-year-old social worker, cast her ballot at about noon on Monday at a Marawi precinct heavily guarded by the Philippine military. The city, parts of which have been rebuilt in recent years, had many checkpoints and roadblocks, she said.

“You can’t help but feel worried because when you see a lot of soldiers, they are preparing for conflict,” said Ms. Lao, whose ancestral home was laid to rubble during the 2017 siege. “I was hesitant to go out and vote.”

She noted that the region remained home to groups affiliated with the Islamic State and added, “This vote is meant for us to choose our leaders who will help rebuild.”

Farther south, the city of Cotabato, the seat of the autonomous government, was under the control of the Philippine Commission on Elections. That takeover followed the shootout and another episode, in which a suspect was injured after a homemade bomb that he was carrying prematurely exploded, said George Garcia, the commission’s chairman.

The authorities also found that some ballots had been tampered with in the remote municipality of Maluso on Basilan Island, he said.

“We determined, as of last night, ballots in 36 out of the 68 precincts had been compromised,” he told reporters in a text message, noting that the names on the ballots had already been chosen in advance.
